title: Velo
subtitle: A Learning Platform Built From the Ground Up

blocks.text: Some details of this case study are intentionally redacted to honor an NDA

blocks.html: "I don't have time to watch 200 hours of video"

Most photography and videography courses are built the same way: <mark>hours of recorded lecture</mark>, then a <mark>quiz to check the box</mark>. Nobody retains anything, and nobody ever finishes them. We had a specific mission: borrow what actually works in <mark>language learning courses</mark> - short lessons, forced engagement, spaced repetition - and apply it to a skill nobody had tried teaching that way before: photography.
A learning platform, not just a course.

We designed and built the <mark>entire system</mark>: research-backed lesson structure, an <mark>interactive camera simulator</mark> students can practice on before touching their own gear, a <mark>custom quiz engine</mark>, <mark>tiered checkout</mark>, and a <mark>dashboard</mark> that always shows where a student stands. It grew into something bigger than one course - the architecture is now solid enough that the team is evaluating it as a licensable <mark>course-building platform</mark> for other creators.

items: <mark>Fully custom platform </mark>- checkout, dashboard, quiz engine, Q&A, camera simulator
<mark>Custom WordPress/Bricks plugin architecture</mark> supporting dynamic lesson hierarchies, adaptive quiz scoring, and tiered content locking
<mark>93% completion rate</mark> and <mark>4.7–4.8/5 average scores</mark> across <mark>UI, navigation, and simplicity</mark> in an 18-person closed beta.

blocks.html: Domain immersion before talking to anyone.

Before writing a single interview question, I audited the market - Duolingo, MasterClass, Udemy to better understand audience and tone. I found out users on reddit preferred <mark>premium and minimal</mark> UI over playful, <mark>functionality over polish</mark>, <mark>desktop-first</mark> since the interactive tools couldn't be compromised for mobile, and lessons framed around <mark>outcomes, not topics</mark> - "shoot any subject in any light," not "the exposure triangle."
4 interviews, deliberately mismatched.

We tested that thesis against people who didn't agree with each other. A session musician who wanted to know why before how. A hobbyist in rural Ohio worried about pacing and video length. A marketing-minded photographer skeptical of course creators in general. A non-photographer who'd never held a camera and only shot on her phone.
Interview Insights

items: Students <mark>disengage without context</mark>, but only want enough of it to stay confident, not overwhelmed
<mark>Gamified streaks and mascots read as childish</mark>, even though instant feedback on quizzes was appreciated
Strongest reaction was to a rough prototype of the <mark>camera simulator concept</mark>; it became the platform's key feature
Current course platforms are <mark>cluttered and confusing</mark>

blocks.html: Deliberately broad user base.

<mark>Beginners and intermediates spanning business use to pure hobbyists</mark> - product photography for a small business on one end, improving your own social content on the other. Since this is a basic course, it will be focused on general techniques that can help a wide variety of users. All users, regardless of occupation described the same core need: <mark>confidence with a physical tool</mark>.
How do we design a course people actually finish, without falling into either passive lecture video or the childish gamification?
I ideated solutions to users' pain points.

items.solution: Minimal, dark, desktop-first, intuitive, collapsible navigation

items.problem: Wanted to know the "Why", without feeling overwhelmed

blocks.html: We mapped out the user flow.

We created an end-to-end user flow before development started - covering dashboard navigation, the camera simulator interaction states, knowledge check scoring logic, and the full assignment review loop.
Key Features
1. Interactive Camera-Settings Simulator

Adjust <mark>key camera settings</mark> (aperture, shutter speed, and ISO) and watch a real photo change <mark>live</mark>. It simulates actual conditions - switch <mark>lighting scenarios</mark>, shoot <mark>handheld or tripod</mark>, get <mark>instant feedback</mark> if a shot would blur or blow out. <mark>Reusable anywhere</mark> - embedded in a lesson or a one-click popup. <mark>Free and account-free</mark> on the landing page, so anyone can try it first.
2. A quiz engine that gives feedback without giving answers.
3. Collapsable, ultra-intuitive navigation.
4. Hoverable Definitions.
Hover over key terms to see what they mean.
5. Digestible content in small chunks & deliberate repetition.
Cover the same information in two formats: video & text to make sure users understand it. This method turned out to be highly effective during beta testing.
Beta testing results.
Future opportunities.
Research changes the plan.
You can't do everything.
We initially planned on heavily utilizing gamification, and focusing on a specific audience. Research made us change our plans.
Content matters the most.
Ultimately, content quality contributed most to this prototype's success - the deliberate repetition and hoverable definitions made the course highly digestible.
Good architecture outgrows the first use case.

We started by wanting to create a photography course, and ended up with a customizable learning platform - one flexible enough that the team is evaluating it as a licensable course-building platform for other instructors.
